claim: It is feasible to determine high-resolution protein structures by electron crystallography of three-dimensional crystals in an electron cryo-microscope (CryoEM).
source: We demonstrate that it is feasible to determine high-resolution protein structures by electron crystallography of three-dimensional crystals in an electron cryo-microscope (CryoEM).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript showing structure determination of lysozyme.

claim: Lysozyme microcrystals were frozen on an electron microscopy grid.
source: Lysozyme microcrystals were frozen on an electron microscopy grid, and electron diffraction data collected to 1.7 Å resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure performed.

claim: Electron diffraction data from lysozyme microcrystals were collected to 1.7 Å resolution.
source: Lysozyme microcrystals were frozen on an electron microscopy grid, and electron diffraction data collected to 1.7 Å resolution.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported from the experiments.

claim: A single tilt series contains up to 90 individual diffraction patterns collected from a single crystal.
source: A single tilt series contains up to 90 individual diffraction patterns collected from a single crystal with tilt angle increment of 0.1–1° and a total accumulated electron dose less than 10 electrons per angstrom squared.
evidence: This describes the data collection protocol developed and implemented.

claim: Diffraction patterns were collected with tilt angle increment of 0.1–1°.
source: A single tilt series contains up to 90 individual diffraction patterns collected from a single crystal with tilt angle increment of 0.1–1° and a total accumulated electron dose less than 10 electrons per angstrom squared.
evidence: This is a parameter of the data collection protocol.

claim: The total accumulated electron dose was less than 10 electrons per angstrom squared.
source: A single tilt series contains up to 90 individual diffraction patterns collected from a single crystal with tilt angle increment of 0.1–1° and a total accumulated electron dose less than 10 electrons per angstrom squared.
evidence: This is a measured parameter of the data collection protocol.

claim: Data from three crystals were indexed and used for structure determination of lysozyme by molecular replacement.
source: We indexed the data from three crystals and used them for structure determination of lysozyme by molecular replacement followed by crystallographic refinement to 2.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This describes the data processing and structure determination approach.

claim: The structure of lysozyme was refined to 2.9 Å resolution.
source: We indexed the data from three crystals and used them for structure determination of lysozyme by molecular replacement followed by crystallographic refinement to 2.9 Å resolution.
evidence: This is the final resolution achieved in the structure determination.

claim: X-ray crystallography depends on large and well-ordered crystals for diffraction studies.
source: X-ray crystallography depends on large and well-ordered crystals for diffraction studies.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of structural biology.

claim: For every elastic scattering event that contributes to a diffraction pattern there are ∼10 inelastic events that cause beam damage.
source: For every elastic scattering event that contributes to a diffraction pattern there are ∼10 inelastic events that cause beam damage (Henderson, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henderson, 1995.

claim: Large crystals are required to withstand the high levels of radiation damage received during X-ray data collection.
source: Therefore, large crystals are required to withstand the high levels of radiation damage received during data collection (Henderson, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henderson, 1995.

claim: Femtosecond X-ray crystallography uses a very intense pulse of X-rays that yields coherent signal in a time shorter than the destructive response to deposited energy.
source: In an attempt to alleviate this problem, researchers have turned to femtosecond X-ray crystallography (Chapman et al., 2011; Boutet et al., 2012), in which a very intense pulse of X-rays yields coherent signal in a time shorter than the destructive response to deposited energy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2011 and Boutet et al., 2012.

claim: Femtosecond X-ray crystallography requires an extremely large number of crystals (millions).
source: While this technique shows great promise, the current implementation of the technology requires an extremely large number of crystals (millions) and access to sources is still in developmental stages.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of the current state of femtosecond X-ray crystallography.

claim: Electrons interact with materials more strongly than X-rays.
source: Because electrons interact with materials more strongly than X-rays (Henderson, 1995), electrons can yield meaningful data from relatively small and thin crystals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Henderson, 1995.

claim: Electrons can yield meaningful data from relatively small and thin crystals.
source: Because electrons interact with materials more strongly than X-rays (Henderson, 1995), electrons can yield meaningful data from relatively small and thin crystals.
evidence: This is inferred from the stronger interaction of electrons with materials.

claim: Electron crystallography has been used successfully to determine the structures of several proteins from thin two-dimensional crystals.
source: This technique has been used successfully to determine the structures of several proteins from thin two-dimensional crystals (2D crystals) (Wisedchaisri et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wisedchaisri et al., 2011.

claim: High energy electrons result in a large amount of radiation damage to the sample, leading to loss in resolution and destruction of the crystalline material.
source: High energy electrons result in a large amount of radiation damage to the sample, leading to loss in resolution and destruction of the crystalline material (Glaeser, 1971).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glaeser, 1971.

claim: Each crystal in electron crystallography can usually yield only a single diffraction pattern.
source: As each crystal can usually yield only a single diffraction pattern, structure determination is only possible by merging data originating from hundreds of individual crystals.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of electron crystallography limitations.

claim: Electron diffraction data from more than 200 individual crystals were merged to generate a data set for aquaporin-0 at 1.9 Å resolution.
source: For example, electron diffraction data from more than 200 individual crystals were merged to generate a data set for aquaporin-0 at 1.9 Å resolution (Gonen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gonen et al., 2005.

claim: Previous attempts at using electron diffraction for structure determination from protein 3D crystals were not successful.
source: While electron crystallography has been successful with 2D crystals, previous attempts at using electron diffraction for structure determination from protein 3D crystals were not successful.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies detailing the difficulties.

claim: Atomic resolution diffraction data can be collected from crystals with volumes up to six orders of magnitude smaller than those typically used for X-ray crystallography.
source: We show here that atomic resolution diffraction data can be collected from crystals with volumes up to six orders of magnitude smaller than those typically used for X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results in the manuscript.

claim: Lysozyme was chosen as a model protein because it is a well-behaved and well-characterized protein that readily forms well-ordered crystals.
source: Lysozyme was chosen as a model protein because it is a well-behaved and well-characterized protein that readily forms well-ordered crystals.
evidence: This is the rationale for the choice of model system.

claim: Lysozyme has been a well-studied protein and the model protein of choice for many new methods in crystallography.
source: From the time its structure was first analyzed (Blake et al., 1962, 1965), lysozyme has been a well-studied protein and the model protein of choice for many new methods in crystallography (Boutet et al., 2012; Cipriani et al., 2012; Nederlof et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies using lysozyme.

claim: Lysozyme microcrystals are up to 6 orders of magnitude smaller in volume than the larger crystals typically used for X-ray crystallography.
source: These specks are up to 6 orders of magnitude smaller in volume than the larger crystals in the drop.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the observed crystal sizes.

claim: More than 100 microcrystals were typically observed per grid preparation.
source: More than 100 microcrystals were typically observed per grid preparation, and these ranged in size from several microns to sub micron.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental preparations.

claim: Lysozyme microcrystals ranged in size from several microns to sub micron.
source: More than 100 microcrystals were typically observed per grid preparation, and these ranged in size from several microns to sub micron.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental observations.

claim: Crystals that appeared thick (estimated as >3 μm) did not yield diffraction data because the electron beam could not penetrate the sample.
source: Crystals that appeared thick (estimated as >3 μm) did not yield diffraction data because the electron beam could not penetrate the sample.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Crystals estimated at ∼1.5 μm showed diffraction, but the quality of the pattern varied depending on the sample tilt.
source: Crystals that appeared slightly thinner, estimated at ∼1.5 μm, did show diffraction, but because the quality of the pattern varied depending on the sample tilt (Figure 2A), we did not use crystals of this thickness and size for data collection.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Approximately 50% of the crystals in the preparations appeared much thinner, estimated at ∼0.5 μm.
source: Approximately 50% of the crystals in our preparations appeared much thinner, estimated at ∼0.5 μm, and showed a distribution of attainable resolutions with the best diffracting to ∼1.7 Å resolution (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental preparations.

claim: The best diffracting thin crystals (∼0.5 μm) diffracted to ∼1.7 Å resolution.
source: Approximately 50% of the crystals in our preparations appeared much thinner, estimated at ∼0.5 μm, and showed a distribution of attainable resolutions with the best diffracting to ∼1.7 Å resolution (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the diffraction experiments.

claim: High quality diffraction data could only be obtained from very thin crystals, ∼0.5–1 μm thick and 1–6 µm long and wide.
source: Generally, we were only able to obtain high quality diffraction data from the very thin crystals, ∼0.5–1 μm thick and 1–6 µm long and wide.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations.

claim: Thin lysozyme crystals (∼0.5–1 μm) contain approximately 55 × 10^6 unit cells.
source: While these crystals are exceptionally small, they still contain approximately 55 × 106 unit cells.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the crystal dimensions and unit cell parameters.

claim: For thin crystals, tilt had no significant adverse effect on the diffraction quality.
source: Moreover, we found that for such thin crystals the tilt had no significant adverse affect on the diffraction quality (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In 2D electron crystallography, the electron dose typically used in diffraction causes significant radiation damage to the sample, leading to a rapid loss in resolution and destruction of the crystal.
source: For 2D electron crystallography, the electron dose that is typically used in diffraction causes significant radiation damage to the sample, leading to a rapid loss in resolution and destruction of the crystal (Glaeser, 1971; Unwin and Henderson, 1975; Taylor and Glaeser, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Glaeser, 1971; Unwin and Henderson, 1975; Taylor and Glaeser, 1976.

claim: 3D crystals can deliver electron diffraction data to atomic resolution with very low doses.
source: However, 3D crystals can deliver electron diffraction data to atomic resolution with very low doses.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results and a citation to Baker et al., 2010.

claim: A recent study documents ∼3 Å resolution diffraction data from catalase 3D crystals after a single exposure of less than 10e−/Å2.
source: A recent study documents ∼3 Å resolution diffraction data from catalase 3D crystals after a single exposure of less than 10e−/Å2 (Baker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baker et al., 2010.

claim: Diffraction data from lysozyme microcrystals could be recorded with extremely low electron dose of <0.01 e−/Å2 per second showing strong and sharp diffraction spots extending well beyond the 2 Å resolution mark.
source: We found that even with extremely low electron dose of <0.01 e−/Å2 per second, we could record diffraction data from lysozyme microcrystals showing strong and sharp diffraction spots extending well beyond the 2 Å resolution mark (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There were no observable adverse effects on resolution or intensity until the accumulated dose had reached ∼9 e−/Å2.
source: There were no observable adverse effects on resolution (Figure 2D) or intensity until the accumulated dose had reached ∼9 e−/Å2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the dose experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The data collection protocol was optimized to keep the total accumulated electron dosage below ∼9 e−/Å2.
source: We therefore optimized the data collection protocol to keep the total accumulated electron dosage below this critical value.
evidence: This is a description of the optimized protocol based on the dose experiment.

claim: By using low dose, multiple diffraction patterns could be collected from a single crystal instead of just a single pattern.
source: By using such a low dose, we could limit the radiation damage to the crystal, allowing us to collect multiple diffraction patterns from a single crystal instead of just a single pattern.
evidence: This is an inference from the low dose approach and experimental results.

claim: Up to 90 individual diffraction patterns could be collected from a single crystal.
source: Using this modified procedure, we were able to collect up to 90 individual diffraction patterns from a single crystal (Video 1).
evidence: This is a result from the experiments shown in Video 1.

claim: Each diffraction pattern was recorded following a 1° tilt to cover ∼40–90°.
source: Each pattern was recorded following a 1° tilt to cover ∼40–90° (begin with the stage tilted at −45° and proceed to collect data to +45° in order to cover a 90° wedge).
evidence: This is a description of the data collection protocol.

claim: Each exposure lasted up to 10 s at a dosage of approximately 0.01 e−/Å2 per second.
source: Each exposure lasted up to 10 s at a dosage of approximately 0.01 e−/Å2 per second, for a cumulative dose of no more than ∼9 e−/Å2 per data set.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection parameters.

claim: The cumulative dose was no more than ∼9 e−/Å2 per data set.
source: Each exposure lasted up to 10 s at a dosage of approximately 0.01 e−/Å2 per second, for a cumulative dose of no more than ∼9 e−/Å2 per data set.
evidence: This is a measured parameter of the data collection.

claim: The unit cell dimensions were calculated as a = b = 77 Å, c = 37 Å, α = β = γ = 90° and P43212 symmetry.
source: The unit cell dimensions were calculated as a = b = 77 Å, c = 37 Å, α = β = γ = 90° and P43212 symmetry.
evidence: This is a result from the data processing and indexing.

claim: The space group symmetry and unit cell dimensions are consistent with previous lysozyme X-ray diffraction data.
source: This space group symmetry and unit cell dimensions are consistent with previous lysozyme X-ray diffraction data (Diamond, 1974; Sauter et al., 2001; Cipriani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous lysozyme structures.

claim: The electron beam wavelength is 0.025 Å at 200 kV.
source: The electron beam wavelength is 0.025 Å at 200 kV compared with ∼1 Å for X-rays.
evidence: This is a known physical property of electrons at 200 kV.

claim: The Ewald sphere in the experiments is nearly flat (the sphere is off the reciprocal plane by only 0.003 Å−1 at 2 Å resolution).
source: Under such conditions, the Ewald sphere in our experiments is nearly flat (the sphere is off the reciprocal plane by only 0.003 Å−1 at 2 Å resolution) even in the high-resolution range.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the electron wavelength and geometry.

claim: The reflections in the experiments are very tight, spreading less than a 6 pixel sphere that corresponds to ∼1/1000 Å.
source: Measurements of the full width at half maximum intensity for the strongest reflections indicate that the reflections in our experiments are very tight, spreading less than a 6 pixel sphere that corresponds to ∼1/1000 Å. (Figure 5)
evidence: This is a measurement from the diffraction data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Multiple observations were recorded for every lattice point.
source: Because we densely sampled the reciprocal space, we recorded multiple observations for every lattice point (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result of the data collection strategy shown in Table 1.

claim: The multiplicity value was 34.
source: Therefore, we could sample the observed intensity values for each reflection multiple times (multiplicity value = 34), and we made the assumption that the strongest intensity roughly approximated the complete intensity.
evidence: This is a statistic from the data processing shown in Table 1.

claim: The merging of data in P422 symmetry from three separate crystals resulted in a final data set with 2490 unique reflections with ∼92% cumulative completeness at 2.9 Å resolution.
source: The merging of data in P422 symmetry from three separate crystals processed in this manner resulted in a final data set with 2490 unique reflections with ∼92% cumulative completeness at 2.9 Å resolution (Table 1, Video 3).
evidence: This is a result from the data processing shown in Table 1 and Video 3.

claim: The structure of lysozyme was solved at 2.9 Å resolution by molecular replacement using the lysozyme PDB 4AXT as a search model.
source: The structure of lysozyme was solved at 2.9 Å resolution by molecular replacement (MR) using the lysozyme PDB 4AXT (Cipriani et al., 2012) as a search model.
evidence: This is a description of the structure determination method.

claim: The initial MR 2Fobs−Fcalc map prior to refinement shows well-defined density around the model, indicating high quality phases from MR.
source: The map shows well-defined density around the model, indicating high quality phases from MR (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the electron density map shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: A composite-omit map showed good agreement with the original map obtained by MR.
source: Likewise, a composite-omit map that was calculated by omitting 5% at a time showed good agreement with the original map obtained by MR (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an observation from the composite-omit map shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When a poly-alanine model of lysozyme was used for MR, the resulting map showed significant density beyond the alanine side chains.
source: When a poly-alanine (polyA) model of lysozyme was used for MR, the resulting map showed significant density beyond the alanine side chains (indicated by arrows in Figure 6E,F), into which the correct side chains could be built.
evidence: This is an observation from the electron density map shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: The MR solution was not dominated by model bias.
source: These results indicated that our solution from MR was not dominated by model bias.
evidence: This is an inference from the poly-alanine MR results.

claim: Following refinement, a solution was found with Rwork/Rfree = 25.5%/27.8% and good geometry at 2.9 Å resolution.
source: Following refinement that included the use of electron scattering factors, rigid body, simulated annealing, and B-factor refinement, a solution was found with acceptable statistics (Rwork/Rfree = 25.5%/27.8%) and good geometry at 2.9 Å resolution (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the crystallographic refinement shown in Table 1.

claim: The final structure has a very low RMSD (0.475 Å for Cα, 0.575 Å for all atoms) when compared to the previously published high-resolution structure of lysozyme.
source: Additionally, the final structure has a very low RMSD (0.475 Å for Cα, 0.575 Å for all atoms) when compared to the previously published high-resolution structure of lysozyme (Cipriani et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison calculation between the MicroED structure and a reference structure.

claim: Only the dataset containing the correct observed experimental intensities yielded a solution that could be further refined to acceptable Rwork/Rfree and geometry.
source: Only dataset 5, which contained the correct observed experimental intensities, yielded a solution that could be further refined to acceptable Rwork/Rfree and geometry.
evidence: This is a result from the model validation tests shown in Table 2.

claim: Datasets containing random errors either did not yield MR solutions or would not allow refinement to produce an acceptable structure.
source: Datasets 1–4, which contained the random errors described above, either did not yield MR solutions or would not allow refinement to produce an acceptable structure (Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the model validation tests shown in Table 2.

claim: None of the unrelated structures gave an acceptable MR solution.
source: None of these structures gave an acceptable MR solution.
evidence: This is a result from the MR validation tests shown in Table 3.

claim: The extracted intensities are accurate enough to yield a reliable structure.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that the extracted intensities are accurate enough to yield a reliable structure and that model bias originating from MR did not skew our results.
evidence: This is an inference from the validation tests.

claim: Model bias originating from MR did not skew the results.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that the extracted intensities are accurate enough to yield a reliable structure and that model bias originating from MR did not skew our results.
evidence: This is an inference from the validation tests.

claim: Data sets collected in electron crystallography of 2D crystals suffer from a missing cone due to the limitation of the maximum achievable tilt angle in the TEM.
source: Data sets collected in electron crystallography of 2D crystals suffer from a missing cone due to the limitation of the maximum achievable tilt angle in the TEM.
evidence: This is established knowledge in electron crystallography.

claim: With tilt angles up to 60°, the missing cone is roughly 13%.
source: Previous reports estimate that with tilt angles up to 60°, the missing cone is roughly 13% (Glaeser et al., 1989), and the resolution in plane is typically higher than the resolution perpendicular to the tilt axis (z*).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glaeser et al., 1989.

claim: Because the data from 3 crystals were used and the orientation of each crystal on the grid varied, the full reciprocal space could be covered.
source: In our experiments, because the data from 3 crystals were eventually used, and the orientation of each crystal on the grid varied, we could cover the full reciprocal space (Video 3).
evidence: This is an inference from the data collection strategy shown in Video 3.

claim: Dynamic scattering likely introduces inaccuracies in the electron diffraction data.
source: Dynamic scattering likely introduces inaccuracies in the electron diffraction data.
evidence: This is a speculation based on known properties of electron diffraction.

claim: In electron diffraction, dynamic scattering could redistribute primary reflection intensities, reducing the accuracy of the intensity measurements.
source: In electron diffraction, dynamic scattering (multi scattering events) could redistribute primary reflection intensities, reducing the accuracy of the intensity measurements by randomly contributing to the observed intensities (Grigorieff et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grigorieff et al., 1996.

claim: Very weak reflections were observed at the positions where systematic absences were expected.
source: However, very weak reflections were observed at the positions where absences were expected (Figure 8).
evidence: This is an observation from the diffraction data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The weak reflections at systematic absence positions likely originate from dynamic scattering events.
source: It is likely that these reflections originate from dynamic scattering events.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of weak reflections at systematic absence positions.

claim: On average, the intensity in the systematic absences was found to be 4.9% of the total intensity of the adjacent spots.
source: On average, the intensity in the systematic absences was found to be 4.9% of the total intensity of the adjacent spots. (Standard deviation 2.7%, Max 12.4%, n = 17).
evidence: This is a measurement from the diffraction data analysis.

claim: Comparison of experimental intensities with intensities obtained by X-ray diffraction of lysozyme indicates that the data follow a similar trend and are not dominated by intensity randomness.
source: Moreover, comparison of our experimental intensities with intensities obtained by X-ray diffraction of lysozyme of the same crystal form indicates that our data follow a similar trend and are not dominated by intensity randomness.
evidence: This is a comparison analysis between MicroED and X-ray data.

claim: A Pearson correlation coefficient between the MicroED and X-ray data sets was 0.63 from 6.0 to 13.5 Å (0.56 from 2.0–13.5 Å).
source: A Pearson correlation coefficient between the two data sets was 0.63 from 6.0 to 13.5 Å (0.56 from 2.0–13.5 Å), indicating conservation of reflection hierarchy—strong intensities remain strong and weak intensities remain weak.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis comparing MicroED and X-ray data.

claim: Multiple scattering contributes at maximum roughly 10% to the intensity value.
source: Together, our analyses suggest that multiple scattering contributes at maximum roughly 10% to the intensity value and that at least for structure determination at 2.9 Å resolution such an error in intensity appears to be tolerable.
evidence: This is an inference from the systematic absence analysis.

claim: At 2.9 Å resolution, an error of roughly 10% in intensity from multiple scattering appears to be tolerable.
source: Together, our analyses suggest that multiple scattering contributes at maximum roughly 10% to the intensity value and that at least for structure determination at 2.9 Å resolution such an error in intensity appears to be tolerable.
evidence: This is an inference from the successful structure determination despite multiple scattering.

claim: It is possible that dynamic scattering will become a significant source of error at higher resolutions.
source: It is possible that dynamic scattering will become a significant source of error at higher resolutions and some correction algorithm will then have to be developed.
evidence: This is a speculation about future challenges at higher resolution.

claim: MicroED should be widely applicable to both soluble and membrane proteins as long as small, well-ordered crystals can be obtained.
source: It should be widely applicable to both soluble and membrane proteins as long as small, well-ordered crystals can be obtained.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential applicability of the method.

claim: Diffraction data at atomic resolution can be collected from crystals that are up to 6 orders of magnitude smaller in volume than those typically used for X-ray crystallography.
source: We have shown that diffraction data at atomic resolution can be collected and a structure determined from crystals that are up to 6 orders of magnitude smaller in volume than those typically used for X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: Electron diffraction of microcrystals offers an alternative when crystal size optimization becomes an impassable barrier.
source: Electron diffraction of microcrystals as described here offers an alternative, allowing this roadblock to be bypassed and data to be collected directly from the initial crystallization hits.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential application of the method.

claim: Better programs need to be developed for accurately determining lattice parameters, indexing all reflections, extracting the intensities and correcting for incomplete intensities, dynamic scattering, and Ewald sphere curvature.
source: Better programs need to be developed for accurately determining lattice parameters, indexing all reflections, extracting the intensities and correcting for incomplete intensities, dynamic scattering, and Ewald sphere curvature.
evidence: This is a discussion of future improvements needed for the method.

claim: Developing procedures for postrefinement should allow for the proper correction and scaling of partially recorded reflections, leading to improved estimation of full intensities.
source: Specifically, developing procedures for postrefinement (unit cell refinement, estimating the mosaic spread, rocking curve, etc) should allow for the proper correction and scaling of partially recorded reflections, leading to improved estimation of full intensities.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential improvements to the method.

claim: Relatively minor modifications to existing programs such as MOSFLM should allow the handling of electron diffraction data from 3D crystals.
source: Relatively minor modifications to existing programs such as MOSFLM (Leslie and Powell, 2007) should allow the handling of electron diffraction data from 3D crystals and take advantage of the large body of work already dedicated to processing X-ray diffraction data.
evidence: This is a speculation about adapting existing software for MicroED data.

claim: Crystal oscillation or related methods such as precession of the electron beam would allow more accurate determination of spot intensities, especially at very high resolutions.
source: Crystal oscillation or related methods such as precession of the electron beam (Gjønnes et al., 1998) would allow more accurate determination of spot intensities, especially at very high resolutions.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential improvements to the data collection method.

claim: It is possible that in electron crystallography dynamic scattering could hinder phasing by heavy metal methods.
source: It is possible that in electron crystallography dynamic scattering could hinder phasing by such methods, and new algorithms will need to be developed to make this possible.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential challenges for phasing methods.

claim: Phase extension from projection maps or from low-resolution density maps can be used for direct phasing.
source: Phase extension from projection maps or from low-resolution density maps can also be used for direct phasing (Gipson et al., 2011; Wisedchaisri and Gonen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gipson et al., 2011 and Wisedchaisri and Gonen, 2011.

claim: Single particle cryo-EM could be used for direct phasing as previously demonstrated where a low-resolution single particle map was used to phase X-ray diffraction data.
source: It is also possible that single particle cryo-EM could be used for direct phasing as previously demonstrated where a low-resolution single particle map was used to phase X-ray diffraction data (Speir et al., 1995; Dodson, 2001; Xiong, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Speir et al., 1995; Dodson, 2001; Xiong, 2008.

claim: Three-dimensional electron diffraction can yield an accurate protein structure from microcrystals.
source: This first study serves as a proof of principle that three-dimensional electron diffraction can yield an accurate protein structure from microcrystals.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the study.

claim: MicroED promises to advance the field of structural biology and open the door to many exciting new studies.
source: As additional protocols and programs are developed, MicroED promises to advance the field of structural biology and open the door to many exciting new studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about the future impact of the method.

claim: All electron microscopy was performed on a FEI Tecnai F20 TEM equipped with a field emission electron source (FEG) and operating at 200 kV.
source: All electron microscopy was performed on a FEI Tecnai F20 TEM equipped with a field emission electron source (FEG) and operating at 200 kV.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental equipment used.

claim: Electron diffraction pattern tilt series data were recorded with a bottom mount TVIPS F416 4 k × 4 k CMOS camera with pixel size 15.6 μm.
source: Electron diffraction pattern tilt series data were recorded with a bottom mount TVIPS F416 4 k × 4 k CMOS camera with pixel size 15.6 μm using built in series exposure mode.
evidence: This is a description of the detector used for data collection.

claim: The FEG can generate a very coherent beam with an energy-spread function of <1 eV at 200 kV acceleration voltage.
source: The FEG can generate a very coherent beam with an energy-spread function of <1 eV at 200 kV acceleration voltage.
evidence: This is a specification of the electron source used.

claim: Phaser was used to obtain phases with lysozyme structure 4AXT as a MR search model (LLG = 372 and TFZ = 14.7).
source: Phaser (McCoy et al., 2007) was used to obtain phases with lysozyme structure 4AXT (Cipriani et al., 2012) as a MR search model (LLG = 372 and TFZ = 14.7).
evidence: This is a description of the molecular replacement procedure and results.

claim: The structure was refined using CNS and PHENIX by rounds of rigid body, simulated annealing, and B-factor refinement.
source: The structure was then refined using CNS (Brünger et al., 1998) and PHENIX (Adams et al., 2010) by rounds of rigid body, simulated annealing, and B-factor refinement.
evidence: This is a description of the refinement procedure.

claim: The Rfree data set represented 10% of the total data set.
source: The Rfree data set represented 10% of the total data set.
evidence: This is a description of the cross-validation procedure used in refinement.

claim: Electron scattering factors were used during refinement.
source: Electron scattering factors (Gonen et al., 2005) were used during refinement.
evidence: This is a description of the refinement procedure with citation to Gonen et al., 2005.

claim: The structure factors and coordinates of the final model were deposited in the Protein Data Bank with accession code 3J4G.
source: The structure factors and coordinates of the final model were deposited in the Protein Data Bank with accession code 3J4G.
evidence: This is information about data deposition.

claim: The in house developed program for processing MicroED data is available for download at http://www.github.com/gonenlab/microED.git.
source: The in house developed program that was used for processing the MicroED data is available for download at http://www.github.com/gonenlab/microED.git.
evidence: This is information about software availability.

claim: Lysozyme microcrystals have length and width that varied from 2 to 6 µm with an estimated thickness of ∼0.5–1 µm.
source: The length and width of the crystals varied from 2 to 6 µm with an estimated thickness of ∼0.5–1 µm.
